summary: Genomic foundation models provide variant-level evidence, but connecting that evidence to phenotype hypotheses requires accounting for uncertainty throughout structured reasoning. We introduce an uncertainty-conditioned path-energy framework that converts sequence predictions and calibrated predictive uncertainty into explicit distributions over graph-supported phenotype hypotheses, without patient-level phenotype supervision. An interpretable learned energy scores admissible gene--disease--phenotype routes, query uncertainty controls the target temperature, and path probabilities are aggregated into phenotype hypotheses. This formulation makes evidence quality an explicit determinant of hypothesis breadth while retaining traceable multi-path support. Exact normalization over enumerable candidate sets provides a reference for evaluating a Hastings-corrected learned revision operator. On AlzKB and Hetionet, phenotype-level entropy tracks upstream uncertainty, with Spearman correlations of 0.951 and 0.878, respectively; ablations identify the contribution of uncertainty conditioning. In masked-edge recovery, the model exceeds chance and degree-matched probability-permutation controls. Training the energy under the uncertainty-dependent temperature yields higher held-out recall@10 than training under a constant temperature of comparable magnitude. Under gene hold-out, recall@10 exceeds that of a trained DistMult embedding on 24 of 30 graph masks (0.183 versus 0.123); this difference is attributable mainly to three genes with many variants and is not established for all genes. These results establish an uncertainty-aware interface from genomic predictions to graph-supported phenotype hypotheses that combines interpretable probability allocation with held-out association recovery of explicitly stated scope.

summary: Medical vision--language models (VLMs) often need to identify small, subtle lesions within high-resolution images containing extensive normal anatomy and redundant visual information. Visual-token compression improves efficiency, but preserving salient regions alone can discard the context needed for diagnostic interpretation. This context can extend across images: in bilateral mammography, the opposite breast provides a patient-specific anatomical reference. Yet retaining such evidence does not ensure that the model uses it effectively. We propose Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning (BESR), which connects evidence preservation with comparative assessment through a bilateral-guided token selector and a bilateral reward. Under a shared token budget, the selector jointly prioritizes lesion appearance and its local and bilateral context, while the reward encourages assessments that benefit from the preserved comparison. Experiments on a bilateral dataset constructed from CBIS-DDSM and on VinDr-Mammo demonstrate improved evidence retention and diagnostic performance under constrained visual-token budgets. Inference benchmarking further shows reduced prefill latency.
title: Bilateral Evidence Selection and Reasoning for Mammography Vision--Language Models

summary: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Overdue-Lin/WAMotor
title: WAMotor: Accelerating World Action Models via Speculative Inference under Dual Nonuniform Denoising Dynamics

summary: The Westphalian assumption that states hold an exclusive, territorially bounded monopoly over legitimate organized violence no longer describes how coercion is organized in the 2020s. This article examines five interlocking classes of non-Westphalian actors (independent military contractors, corporate private military and security companies, defense-technology neo-contractors, cyber-mercenaries or private sector offensive actors, and hybrid trans-sovereign military orders) across four functional domains: strategic, infrastructural, algorithmic and cognitive. It builds the analysis on four frameworks: liquid state systems, flow sovereignty, Dual-Core Fractal Statecraft and melting cartographies. It is explicit that the last two are synthesized from documented components rather than taken from a settled canon. Empirically, the article documents a structural inflection between 2020 and late 2026. Labour-intensive guarding conglomerates remain large, but strategic leverage is moving to capital- and software-intensive firms whose code sits inside kill chains, orbital links and national registries. Case studies run from Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mozambique to the Wagner/Africa Corps portfolio, Belt and Road corridor guardians, commercial spyware and zero-day markets, Red Sea chokepoints, cloud evacuation and orbital geofencing. Legally, the article identifies an inverse law of sovereign accountability: participation falls as bindingness rises, leaving governance split between voluntary soft law and private quasi-export controls. It closes with a four-pillar blueprint for constrained liquid sovereignty: modernized jurisdiction and attribution, hardened cyber supply-chain controls, publicly anchored compute and connectivity, and constitutional guardrails against moral crumple zones. KSCCN article in the Liquid State series. It applies the framework of "From Territorial Monopoly to Flow Sovereignty" (10.5281/zenodo.24298572) to non-state force, and is a companion to "The Liquid Military Order" (10.5281/zenodo.24354669), "The Liquid Sovereign" (10.5281/zenodo.24378053) and the Volume I inventory "Status Update: The Liquid State Framework" (10.5281/zenodo.24377832). This full-colour edition has 25 figures (five original visualisations and twenty added figures, including five maps), five tables and 289 Harvard references. Maps use Natural Earth boundaries for orientation only and imply no position on any territorial claim. A PDF and an editable DOCX are provided.

summary: # A counterfactual attribution framework for separating fire weather and human ignition in satellite active-fire trends   This archive contains the code and derived data for a counterfactual attribution framework that separates the effect of fire weather from that of human ignition in satellite active-fire records. The framework is applied to MODIS records for Jiangxi Province, China, from 2003 to 2024, and the archive reproduces every result of that application.   Human ignition is not recorded in any dataset, so the framework estimates it indirectly. A model of daily fire occurrence is fitted on a 0.1° grid using fire weather and static environmental covariates only, with no year, time index or other trending variable. Leave-one-winter-out cross-validation gives the number of fire grid-days expected from the weather of each winter, and the ratio of observed to expected counts measures what fire weather does not explain. Down-sampled controls are corrected back to population-scale probabilities, and covariates are clipped to the training range before prediction so that trending inputs cannot cause extrapolation. The residual is then checked without any model, by comparing occurrence rates within bins of the Fire Weather Index (FWI), and against sensor degradation, faster suppression and vegetation greening.   Before modelling, a screen removes persistent daytime warm-season anomalies (PDWA): fixed 1 km pixels that are detected in many summers but almost never at night or in winter. These are solar-heated surfaces rather than fires.   To apply the framework elsewhere, replace the inputs listed in Section 1.2 and the provincial boundary, and review the PDWA thresholds (Section 3).   The archive has two folders:   ``` code/      Python pipeline that produces every number, table and figure dataset/   derived data: screened fire detections, grid definition and the tables behind each figure and table ```   ---   ## 1. code/   ``` code/   src/               analysis scripts, numbered in run order, plus four shared modules     jxconfig.py      all input and output paths (edit this first, or set the environment variables it lists)     fwi.py           Canadian Forest Fire Weather Index System (FFMC, DMC, DC, ISI, BUI, FWI)     stats_utils.py   Mann-Kendall, Pettitt, Theil-Sen and circular statistics     plotstyle.py     figure style (Times New Roman; PNG at 600 dpi and vector PDF)   requirements.txt   package versions the results were produced with (Python 3.9)   LICENSE            MIT ```   ### 1.1 Environment   Python 3.9. Install the dependencies with   ``` pip install -r requirements.txt ```   The heaviest steps are the climate extraction (about 90 GB of netCDF read once) and the LightGBM attribution (about 8 GB of memory). A complete run from the raw inputs takes on the order of a day. Steps `01`–`19` build the intermediate products and need to be run only once; the analysis scripts after that can be rerun independently.   The netCDF4 library cannot open files whose path contains non-ASCII characters on Windows, so keep the data and output directories on ASCII paths.   ### 1.2 Input data   All inputs are public and are not redistributed here. Download them and point `src/jxconfig.py` at them, either by editing `ROOT` or through the environment variables `JX_ROOT`, `JX_DATA`, `JX_INTERIM`, `JX_OUT`, `JX_FIG`, `JX_FIRE_GPKG`, `JX_NDVI` and `JX_FVC`.   | Dataset | Content | Source | |---|---|---| | MODIS C6.1 active fire (MCD14ML) | 1 km fire detections | https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/download/ | | VIIRS S-NPP VNP14IMG | 375 m fire detections | https://firms.modaps.eosdis.nasa.gov/download/ | | CMFD V2.0 |

summary: This deposit accompanies the article “Adaptive continuation and classification of codimension-two equilibrium bifurcations”. It provides the Python implementation, numerical CSV datasets, original figures and supplementary material needed to reproduce the reported calculations. The workflow combines equilibrium continuation, spectral tracking, augmented-system refinement and local bifurcation classification. Seven worked applications are accompanied by an external Hopf reference problem, transformed normal-form benchmarks, independent reference checks, controller sensitivity experiments, classification margins and optional derivative-consistency checks. A documented driver regenerates the numerical outputs and figures. A browser atlas covers all seven application cases and their critical-point diagnostics. A separate JavaScript laboratory illustrates five models. Both support CSV export. The implementation uses floating-point arithmetic with NumPy and SciPy. Zero–Hopf and Hopf–Hopf classifications are validated on transformed normal-form benchmarks; FitzHugh–Nagumo supplies an applied generalized Hopf case with an independent return-map check. No directed-rounding interval certification is provided. Original software and software-use documentation are licensed under MIT. Numerical data, original figures, environment records and the supplementary PDF are licensed under CC BY 4.0 International. The archive includes both license texts and specifies their file scopes.

summary: FAIR metadata (Schema.org, Bioschemas and MLCommons Croissant) for the ELIXIR 3D-BioInfo benchmark of 1,677 homodimer interfaces from 1,645 protein crystal structures, together with the structure files (PDB and mmCIF), an in-repository snapshot of the PDB metadata of every entry, the documentation of the label curation, and four homology-aware 5-fold cross-validation splits (CATH/UniProt, MMseqs2, BLASTClust and their union) attached to every interface. The benchmark was published by Schweke et al. (2023, Proteomics 23(17):e2200323, doi:10.1002/pmic.202200323; 836 physiological and 841 non-physiological interfaces). This package uses the curated annotation file of the benchmark authors (844 physiological and 833 non-physiological interfaces; 16 labels revised, 20 interfaces flagged ambiguous and 6 flagged for deletion). Every interface carries both the curated label and the published label ( PublishedPhysio ). See data/curation/README.md . Please cite the original publication as well as this package.

summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in real-world long-horizon manipulation, where memory plays a crucial role. However, existing memory-augmented VLAs either retrieve past observations without reasoning about what they imply, or reason over the full history in a shared context where it crowds out current perception. Cognitive science treats them as distinct systems: memory reconstructs past experience to decide what to do, while perception guides how to act. We therefore propose ActMem, an in-context memory framework that decouples memory reasoning from perceptual grounding within a single vision-language backbone. Built on a vision-language model with native video understanding, ActMem infers the current subtask from a timestamped interaction history and keeps the hidden states formed during this inference as a Latent Memory Chain-of-Thought (Memory CoT), which conditions a flow-matching action expert. Perception Attention further lets the expert attend directly to the current view. To keep inference fast under long histories, Efficient Memory CoT Inference reuses computation across consecutive decisions without changing the output. ActMem achieves 71.1% task success and 80.8% completion success on RoboMemArena, surpassing the strongest baseline by 7.5 and 8.7 percentage points, and 73.8% average success on MIKASA-Robo, the best among all compared methods. In the real world, it reaches 68.8% average success on exogenous, endogenous, and traceless memory tasks, 10.0 percentage points above the strongest memory-augmented VLA. Code and checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/LigphiDonk/ActMem and https://huggingface.co/donk111/ActMem.

summary: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.

summary: Combining fine-tuned models by composing their parameter updates has become a standard alternative to multi-task training. We formalize composability as a property of a collection of task vectors and prove that the excess loss of the merged model is controlled by an interference functional of the cross-task curvature overlap and the signed alignment of the updates. In the quadratic regime this functional equals the excess loss, giving a criterion that is necessary as well as sufficient and that measures the angle between task vectors in the curvature metric rather than the Euclidean one. Fine-tuning under a curvature-guided regularizer -- constructed from curvature statistics of the kind memory-efficient optimizers maintain -- keeps displacement in the base curvature metric below a ceiling set by the penalty coefficient at every iterate, at the standard $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ non-convex rate. Under a single Loewner comparison between the base statistic and the task curvatures, this control converts into a ceiling on the interference functional, inversely proportional to the penalty coefficient, so that the curvature term of the bound is controlled during training. A first-order term, present because regularized solutions are not stationary for the task loss, is not reduced in the same way. Experiments on an exact non-quadratic model confirm the budget and the ceiling, show the first-order term dominating for strong penalties, and find the curvature-guided penalty slightly better than an isotropic one. In a three-seed transformer study the functional is rank-correlated with merging degradation, but no more strongly than the Euclidean displacement norm.

summary: Similarity search is essential to many applications but incurs massive data movement when executed on conventional architectures. Content-addressable memory (CAM) is a promising hardware substrate, as it allows similarity search directly in the CAM array, minimizing data movement and offering both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, conventional CAM array readout produces only binary match results, discarding quantitative similarity information that could be further exploited. Extracting this information requires interpreting the CAM array output voltage that evolves during a CAM search, making the sensing timestamp a crucial design variable alongside the reference voltage and decoding parameter. In this work, we propose RE-CAM, a readout enhancement framework for CAM that is agnostic to memory technology and application, enabling CAM array readout to approximate linear and nonlinear functions with one CAM search. By reusing the comparators to sense the time-varying output voltage multiple times, jointly optimizing the three design variables under system constraints and hardware nonidealities, and co-designing the optimization algorithm and reconfigurable hardware, RE-CAM achieves accurate approximation with low energy and area overhead without introducing a readout throughput bottleneck. Across linear, piecewise-linear, sigmoid, and exponential functions, RE-CAM reduces normalized root mean square error by 10.89% to 24.34% for general approximation and 29.43% to 46.73% when exploiting dataset distribution, compared to a shared uniform-reference ADC baseline with the same comparison budget. Relative to the same baseline, RE-CAM also achieves $8\times$ higher search throughput while reducing energy per search and area by 47% and 39%, respectively.

summary: Neural state-space identification learns dynamical models from measured inputs and outputs. SUBNET combines this task with an encoder that estimates initial states from short measurement histories. Its continuous-time version requires many successive neural-network evaluations during numerical integration, resulting in slow training speed which is a major limitation for practical use cases. We propose deep structured state space models (DS3M), which combine compact nonlinear dynamical components in parallel and in series. Custom GPU kernels implemented with Triton reduce the launch and memory overhead of their sequential evaluation. We explain this construction, describe a port-Hamiltonian variant, and present various benchmark comparisons of accuracy and training time.

summary: Parametric memory allows Large Language Models to internalize knowledge directly into their weights, offering a potentially powerful alternative to retrieval-based memory (RAG). However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

However, existing approaches to parametric memory are difficult to deploy as they largely mirror the Continual Learning (CL) objective of retaining information indefinitely. This is neither sustainable nor sufficient for a memory system, which must govern knowledge across its lifecycle by retaining stable facts, reinforcing recurring observations, updating changed beliefs, and allowing transient information to fade. We propose a system for parametric memory management consisting of a memory substrate (handling information storage and forgetting) and a learned policy (what to remember, how deeply, and for how long). Our substrate is a fixed-capacity LoRA adapter that consists of k-hot rank combinations which store facts without catastrophic interference and maintain an independently controlled temporal decay, enabling outdated information to fade while long-term facts persist. On this substrate, we train a lightweight controller that governs each incoming user event to ensure the memory system reflects the user's true, updated belief state. To evaluate how memory systems manage user memory, we introduce a controlled dataset of long-horizon user trajectories with varying persistence of facts based on changing belief states and user-behavioral shifts, and probe queries that test recall while information is valid and abstention after it expires. Our policy learns to effectively manage user memory over its entire lifecycle, balancing recall and abstention to achieve 86% of oracle performance, unlike CL and RAG baselines that primarily default to one of the two behaviors. By providing the first system to manage memory directly in model weights, this work establishes a foundation for long-horizon parametric memory.

summary: Search, especially top-k similarity search, plays a vital role in many applications, but its performance can be severely limited by memory access overhead. In-memory search (IMS), an alternative to CPU/GPU-based approaches, exploits massive parallelism within a content-addressable memory (CAM) array to perform search in situ and provides both low latency and high energy efficiency. However, the capacity of a single CAM array is often insufficient for modern workloads, requiring data to be distributed across multiple arrays. Deploying scalable top-k similarity search across multiple CAM arrays poses a fundamental problem that existing designs fail to address: how to accurately and efficiently reduce local binary match results to global top-k results. This work introduces CAIMS, a cross-array IMS framework that is agnostic to memory technologies and applications, enabling scalable and efficient top-k similarity search while preserving accuracy. To enable accurate top-k result reduction, CAIMS leverages the existing threshold match functionality with a combined offline and online parameter selection approach to transform local binary match results that lack globally comparable similarity information into global coarse-grained similarity scores. To further improve efficiency, CAIMS conducts hierarchical reduction and transfers only the selection results and necessary control signals with lightweight local peripherals. Implemented on a 3D NAND Flash model and demonstrated using the retrieval phase of retrieval-augmented generation, CAIMS improves throughput by up to $22.3\times/10.1\times$ and energy efficiency by $426.6\times/23.7\times$ compared to the server-class CPU baseline and prior 3D NAND Flash accelerators, respectively, while maintaining comparable accuracy.

summary: Long-horizon LLM agents often exceed their context windows, forcing them to discard information that may be needed later. Existing context management strategies rely on summarization, masking, or structured memory, requiring decisions about what to preserve or how to retrieve it before future needs are known. However, these methods can introduce lossy compression, potentially discarding details needed for future tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce GrepMem, a simple, lossless, and index-free memory mechanism built on two components: an append-only plain-text log of the agent's complete history and a regular-expression search tool for on-demand recall. Unlike structured memory systems, GrepMem requires no embeddings, retrieval index, memory extraction, or additional models. We train Qwen3.5-9B with reinforcement learning under five context management strategies and evaluate on multi-question research sessions, long-stream recall, and agent-trajectory question answering. GrepMem achieves 95-97% accuracy on ContextBench, versus at most 21% for lossy baselines, and outperforms SUPO's summarization by 8.8 percentage points on BCP-Multi. GrepMem scales effectively to increasingly long input streams while remaining on the accuracy-token-cost Pareto frontier across all five evaluation tasks. Our results show that a plain-text log and grep provide a simple but competitive approach to long-horizon agent memory, without requiring complex structured memory infrastructure.

summary: DISCO is a recent internal cluster validity index for density-based clustering that, unlike earlier indices, also evaluates the quality of noise labels. The discoCVI package makes DISCO available in R. This article describes the design of the package and a typical workflow, in which DISCO is used to compare clusterings and to choose the parameters of HDBSCAN without ground truth, followed by the implementation introduced in version 0.2.0. DISCO is defined through density-connectivity distances between all pairs of points, so direct implementations store several n-by-n matrices. We show that every quantity DISCO needs can be read off the single-linkage merge tree of the mutual-reachability minimum spanning tree, so that the index can be computed exactly with memory that grows linearly with the number of points, while the running time remains quadratic as in the original definition. The implementation is tested against the previous version, agrees with the original Python implementation to within $3 \times 10^{-13}$, and corrects the score of singleton clusters to match the published definition. In benchmarks, discoCVI is 23 to 138 times faster than its previous version for 500 to 4,000 points and 3 to 9 times faster than the Python reference for 500 to 8,000 points, using a fraction of the memory of both, and it scores 100,000 points in about 50 seconds with less than 200 MB of memory.

summary: Calibrating a volatility surface from sparse option prices requires repeated solutions of a pricing equation as the volatility parameters change. We implement a hybrid quantum and classical method for this inverse problem using the Dupire local-volatility model. A positive coefficient representation specifies the local variance, and linear combinations of Hamiltonian simulations approximate the associated pricing evolution. The circuit propagates through successive maturity intervals and evaluates discrepancies at the observed strikes. Measurement counts provide the objective values used by a classical optimiser to update the volatility coefficients. We implement this calibration cycle in a logical gate simulator and assess it alongside classical pricing solvers and alternative surface models. Multiple-maturity synthetic examples illustrate the reconstruction of smiles and skews, while a separate small circuit experiment tests the complete measured calibration. The comparisons quantify the effects of model flexibility, pricing approximation and measurement precision. Recorded gate counts and sampling budgets identify the main computational costs of the implementation.

summary: Gate-level netlists circulate among IP integrators and foundries and can be extracted from chips. Reverse engineering them into readable register-transfer-level (RTL) code would help an adversary understand and modify a design, but remains difficult because word-level operations are scattered across many gates. Large language models (LLMs) can write and optimize RTL, but often fail to recover it from a whole netlist. We propose LOCA (LOgic Cone Attack), an LLM-based attack that divides an anonymized netlist into logic cones, has parallel agents rewrite them, and assembles compact RTL. Each cone contains the complete next-state logic of a group of related registers, giving an agent a small, meaningful task. Of five partitioning methods tested, only grouped cones lead to recovery. LOCA keeps only RTL proven equivalent to the netlist and measures its quality by compression. Function-preserving obfuscation does not stop LOCA on the tested designs, whereas unknown keys or hidden cell functions prevent it from proving recovery of the original design. Across 21 model-design pairs, LOCA recovers 17, versus 6 with whole-netlist prompting. Per-run recovery across models rises from 5% to 74%, at a median cost below one dollar with a low-cost model.
title: Verified Netlist-to-RTL Recovery with LLM Agents

summary: Structural symmetry, thermodynamic phase stability, and elastic-wave response provide related but distinct descriptions of a transforming solid. We formulate a symmetry-stratified framework that connects these descriptions through a finite-dimensional internal state and a parent-invariant free energy. Stabilizers classify structural states, whereas free-energy comparisons and stability conditions determine equilibrium branches and dissipative evolution. Equivariance ensures that the frozen elastic tangent inherits the structural stabilizer. Equality requires additional identifiability conditions. Little-group representations and degenerate perturbation theory then determine whether an acoustic doublet splits and the first nonzero splitting order $p$. On a selected continuous branch with order-parameter exponent $β$, a regular, observable acoustic gap scales as $|t|^{pβ}$, provided critical self-energies and structural relaxation do not dominate the measurement. Explicit tensorial and cubic-to-tetragonal realizations yield linear and quadratic splitting channels, together with directionally protected degeneracies. Separate numerical benchmarks examine free-energy reconstruction, coexistence, elastic compatibility, finite-temperature spectra, and controlled critical readouts. Reanalysis of NiTi measurements illustrates effective elastic degeneracy, thermal-history dependence, and the predictive value of independently measured phase fractions. Most importantly, the framework identifies the constitutive and measurement assumptions required to infer structural changes from mechanical spectra.

summary: Geometric confinement changes both thermal relaxation and heat throughput, but these effects need not be governed by the same conduction path. We establish a distinction between serial and parallel geometries for passive, homogeneous Fourier conductors at fixed material properties, volume and length. For a reduced variable-area conductor, two logarithmic shape harmonics independently tune two selected Bloch-rate pairs, and exact local transport level sets permit spectral redistribution at fixed effective diffusivity. A nonperturbative weighted Poincaré bound, however, requires the effective axial diffusivity to vanish if the first positive insulated rate tends to zero at fixed length. This obstruction is avoided by continuous parallel paths with weak transverse exchange. Capacity-weighted networks identify the exchange mechanism, and a three-dimensional product domain provides an exact bulk realization. Its axial conductance remains $κV/L^2$, while exactly one positive insulated rate vanishes and the next approaches a positive limit set by axial, chamber and neck diffusion. The slow rate is asymptotically the transverse neck conductance times the sum of inverse chamber capacities. Spectral projection estimates translate this separation into a preparation- and readout-dependent observation window. The result is metastable retention of a temperature contrast under insulated conditions, not a second equilibrium state. It identifies when geometrical control of internal equilibration can be separated from macroscopic heat transport.

summary: An observable decision reveals the selected action but does not determine which alternatives were internally represented. Drawing on prospection research and hippocampal forward-sweep observations, we develop Before the Choice, an evidence-oriented framework distinguishing future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. Code and protocol records: https://github.com/besionisrael/before-choice
title: Before the Choice: An Evidential Framework for Studying Prospective Representations in Language Models

summary: Identifying the phases of a quantum many-body system as its parameters vary is a central problem in condensed-matter physics. Data-driven approaches address this task by comparing quantum states, for instance through their fidelity, and locating transitions where these comparisons change abruptly. In this work, we introduce the inverse participation ratio (IPR) kernel, a kernel method built for learning quantum phases of matter from IPRs in physically motivated bases. Unlike fidelity-based kernels, the IPR kernel can identify states with physically meaningful similarity even when they are orthogonal. We test the method on ground states of the transverse-field Ising (TFIM) and Heisenberg XXZ models. For TFIM Gibbs states, we further show that the IPR kernel retains phase-relevant structure over a range of nonzero temperatures where the phase signal of fidelity-based kernels is already degraded. More broadly, our results suggest that quantum kernels benefit more from feature maps tailored to the physics of the problem than from maximal expressivity.
title: A Basis-Dependent Kernel for Learning Quantum Phases of Matter

summary: The lack of interoperable data standards among reference genome data-sharing platforms inhibits cross-platform analysis while increasing the risk of data provenance loss. Here, we describe the FAIR-bioHeaders Reference genome (FHR), a metadata standard guided by the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) in addition to the principles of Transparency, Responsibility, User focus, Sustainability, and Technology (TRUST). The objective of FHR is to provide an extensive set of data serialisation methods and minimum data field requirements while still maintaining extensibility, flexibility, and expressivity in an increasingly decentralised genomic data ecosystem. The effort needed to implement FHR is low; FHR's design philosophy ensures easy implementation while retaining the benefits gained from recording both machine and human-readable provenance.
title: FAIR-bioHeaders Specification

summary: Overview The Earth Surface Anomaly dataset (v1.1) is a five-class, event-grouped Sentinel-2 benchmark for immediate disaster and surface-anomaly detection. It contains 622 samples grouped into 46 event or spatiotemporal observation units (17 source-named/inventory units and 29 observation groups, 2017–2025, globally distributed): 129 fire, 58 flood-context, 54 landslide, 204 crop-residue-burning and 177 retrogressive-thaw-slump samples. 595 samples carry source polygon-derived binary masks; 27 carry weak point inventories only; all 54 landslide samples include pre/post paired observations. Industrial heat sources (208 candidates) are excluded from this release and 17 visually ambiguous candidates are withheld, both enumerated in quality/excluded_samples.csv . Sample structure Each sample ( data/CODE/EVENT/SAMPLE/ ) provides a six-band Sentinel-2 L2A chip (declared bands B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, B12; aligned grid spacing does not imply native 10 m for every band), a 0/1 binary mask, RGB/NIR/SWIR previews, annotation.json and measured facts.json (CRS, transform, WGS84 bounds, geometry statistics, spectral indices, SHA256 checksums). Annotation-conditioned vision-language tasks (4–6 per sample depending on label strength and pairing) cover event classification, factual captioning, spatial reasoning, visual grounding, spectral comparison, and for suitable samples temporal reasoning and label provenance. Splits Group splits are precomputed: default splits/event_disjoint (443/102/77 train/val/test) and inherited splits/site_disjoint (433/114/75). Event-disjointness does not guarantee site-disjointness (1 measured case); use site_disjoint when required. Never randomly split patches from the same event. Screening and quality All 639 non-industrial candidates underwent AI-assisted visual screening of RGB, SWIR and target crops with review sheets and per-sample geometry/text audits retained in the release ( quality/ , visual_review.csv ). This is not independent expert pixel adjudication, field validation, or new external verification of every event identity. Limitations (documented in README, README_zh and DATA_DICTIONARY) Flood-context masks often follow existing river channels; no paired baseline establishes incremental inundation. Fire annotations can cover smoke, scars or hotspots and are not universally burned-area boundaries. Crop-residue burning is a source label; imagery alone does not establish fuel identity. Thaw mechanism/onset and landslide onset cannot be established from the supplied views alone. Point inventories (27 samples) are weak localization, not segmentation truth; polygon provenance does not guarantee exact pixel boundaries. Radiometric scale/offset and the inherited non-landslide band mapping have not been independently traced to every source product; facts.json indices are stored-DN calculations, not validated physical reflectance. External event-match references in index/external_verification_ledger.csv were not newly re-verified during release preparation.
